--- title: "Linear Regression" author: " " format: revealjs: theme: default slide-number: true transition: fade code-fold: false execute: echo: true warning: false message: false jupyter: python3 --- ## First: Create Groups in Canvas Find the desk with your group number: **this is the same group number as last and next week** - Log into Canvas - Click on **People** on the right side of the page - Click on **Group** - Scroll to the group with the number on your desk and enroll yourself in the group (Classwork: Science and Data) **NOTE** Remember your Group number for next week, you will have to enroll again! ## Time table {.smaller} | Week | Date | Planned Activity | Delivery | |------------------|:-----------------|-----------------:|:----------------:| | 35 | ~~Wed 26.08~~ | ~~Visualization/Python~~ | ~~Yes (does not count)~~ | | | ~~Fri 28.08~~ | ~~Telling stories~~ | ~~Yes (5 points)~~ | | 36 | ~~Wed 02.09~~ | ~~Visualization/Python~~ | ~~Yes (5 points)~~ | | | ~~Fri 04.09~~ | ~~Science and Data~~ | ~~No~~ | | 37 | ~~Wed 09.09~~ | ~~Homework~~ | ~~No~~ | | | **Fri 11.09** | **Science and Data and Regression** | **Yes (5 points)** | | 38 | Wed 16.09 | Regression | Wed or Fri | | | Fri 18.09 | Regression | Wed or Fri | | *39* | *Wed 23.09* | *Project 1* | *-* | | | *Fri 25.09* | *Project 1* | *First Hand-in* | | *40* | *Wed 30.09* | *Project 1* | *-* | | | *Fri 02.10* | *Project 1* | *Second Hand-in* | ## Plan for today - Classwork: Science and Data - Group discussion about the scientific paper you read at home - Deliver a word file with your answers. This is an assignment worth 5 points - Introducing Regression ## The question **Do children with a mobile phone sleep less?** We will start with a very simple comparison: - **Group 1:** children who have a mobile - **Group 2:** children who do not - **Outcome:** hours of sleep per night --- ## Let's simulate some data We will simulate a fictional dataset - these are not the same data as in the paper! ::: {#fcc688b3 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
parent_education_years mobile sleep_hours
0 13.003075 0 7.563246
1 13.746864 1 6.994161
2 12.314655 1 6.541806
3 10.773520 0 8.570364
4 11.863323 1 7.169482
``` ::: ::: --- ## What do the data look like? ::: {#d4a0b2a1 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](regression1_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){width=663 height=411} ::: ::: --- ## First idea: compare the averages **Calculate the average sleep in each group.** ::: {#71d583de .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
mean std count
mobile
0 7.770903 0.532023 100
1 7.491948 0.488079 140
``` ::: ::: Is the difference large enough when we include also the variation within groups? --- ## A t-test A two-sample t-test asks: > **Is the difference between the two group means large relative to the variation within the groups?** $$ H_0:\mu_{\text{no phone}}=\mu_{\text{phone}} \qquad\text{vs}\qquad H_A:\mu_{\text{no phone}}<\mu_{\text{phone}} $$ ::: {#18679bd8 .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` t = -4.14 p = 0.0000 ``` ::: ::: --- ## But are the groups comparable? Imagine that the two groups differ in more ways than just owning a phone. For example: **Parent's years of education** Brief group discussion: Why might this matter? . . . - It may be that high and low educated parents have different patterns when it comes to buying phones - It may also be the parents education has something to say for the children's sleeping patterns --- ## A potential confounder Let's look at parent education and mobile ownership ::: {#739d7cc7 .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](regression1_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=659 height=411} ::: ::: --- ## A potential confounder Let's look at parent education and sleep. ::: {#59aeca37 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](regression1_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=663 height=429} ::: ::: --- ## Confounding: the key idea A **confounder** is a variable that is related to: 1. the thing we are comparing, and 2. the outcome we care about. Parent education interacts with both _mobile ownership_ and _sleep_ So the mobile/no-mobile comparison can mix together several differences. --- ## So what can we do? We would like to make a **fairer comparison**. Instead of asking: > "How different is sleep between children with and without mobiles?" we can ask: > **"How different is sleep between children with and without mobiles, _after accounting for parent education_?"** **Short group discussion**: What does _after accounting for parent education_ means? --- ## Regression{.smaller} Regression allows us to describe the outcome using several variables. For example: **Sleep = mobile ownership + parent education + other variation** The important idea is: > Each coefficient describes the relationship between a predictor and the outcome **while taking the other predictors into account**. --- ## Simple linear regression{.smaller} A linear regression with only mobile ownership is essentially a group comparison. $$ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i $$ - $y_i$ hours of sleep for child $i$ - $x_i$ mobile ownership (0/1) for child $i$ - $\beta_0, \beta_1$ coefficient to be estimated - $\epsilon_i$ this is the "error" that we assume is _independent and identical distributed_ among all observations Short group discussion: Do you remember what _independent and identical distributed_ means? ## Simple linear regression - Fitted model{.smaller} ::: {#17cde03d .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $$ \widehat{Sleep} = 7.77 -0.28\times Mobile $$ ::: ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Interpretation - $\beta_0$ Average over the whole group: on average the group of children sleeps 7.77 hours per night - $\beta_1$ Difference between not owning and owning a mobile decreases the hours of sleep by 0.28 - Testing for $\beta_1 = 0$ is equivalent to the t-test we had before! ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {#be60a1ff .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](regression1_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=663 height=411} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Adding a potential confounder A linear regression with only mobile ownership is essentially a group comparison. $$ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \epsilon_i $$ - $y_i$ hours of sleep for child $i$ - $x_{1i}$ mobile ownership (0/1) for child $i$ - $x_{2i}$ years of parents education for child $i$ - $\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2$ are model parameters ## The fitted model{.smaller} ::: {#ee2340bf .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} $$ \widehat{Sleep} = 6.22 -0.58\times Mobile +0.14\times ParentEducation $$ ::: ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Interpretation - $\hat{\beta_0} = 6.22$ The predicted sleep when Mobile = 0 and ParentEducation = 0. - $\hat{\beta_1} = −0.58$ children with a mobile are predicted to sleep 0.50 hours less per night than those without a mobile, _holding constant the parents years of education_. - $\beta_2=0.12$ each additional year of parent education is associated with 0.12 additional hours of predicted sleep, _holding constant the mobile ownership_. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {#b67ffb29 .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](regression1_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=663 height=429} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## What does "holding constant" mean? Suppose we compare two children who are similar with respect to parent education: - both have parents with **14 years of education** - one child has a mobile - one child does not Regression asks about the expected difference in their sleep **The mobile coefficient is a comparison after accounting for parent education.** --- ## Comparing the models Let's compare the estimated coefficients for mobile ownership in the two models: ::: {#275acc36 .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Simple linear regression estimate: -0.28 hours Adjusted estimated: -0.58 hours ``` ::: ::: The estimates are different because **mobile ownership and parent education are related in our simulated data**. --- ## What can regression do and what it cannot Regression can adjust for variables that: - we have measured, and - we have included in the model. It cannot automatically fix: - an important confounder we did not measure - poor measurement - a badly specified model - selection problems And: > **Adjustment does not prove causation.** A safer phrase is: **"association after adjustment"** unless the study design and assumptions justify a causal interpretation. ---
